Once all authors sign the AI code form on AirTable, SlackBot will message you an AI disclosure that you should place here. ::: ## Purpose Placeholder. This section will state why the work was done, the key takeaway, and who it is for. The argument to make here: binder design campaigns run with ESMFold2 return mostly α-helical binders, and a designer who needs a different fold has no obvious knob to turn. We add a secondary-structure term to the design loss, show what it buys and what it costs, and report whether the resulting designs are worth trialing. Primary audience: people running structure-prediction-based binder design campaigns, and people interested in what can be steered in a folding model after training. ## Introduction Placeholder. Three claims to establish, each needing citations added to `ref.bib`: 1. **Binder design tends to be α-rich.** Design pipelines built on structure predictors return helical binders far more often than any other fold class. To write: how general this is across pipelines, and what is already known about why. 2. **Increasing structural diversity yields better campaigns.** A more structurally diverse design pool improves the odds that a campaign yields a binder that works experimentally. To write: the evidence for this, and how diversity is usually pursued today. 3. **Sometimes success is locked behind β-rich designs.** Some epitopes are not addressable by a helical bundle. To write: concrete examples where a β-rich binder was the one that worked. These three claims motivate the three questions that structure the rest of the notebook. :::{.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reproducing this notebook"} **This notebook is meant to be reproducible, and the two kinds of input here are treated differently.** The natural binder reference set is derived from a recorded RCSB query, so it is rebuilt rather than shipped: the first execution on a fresh clone downloads about 400 MB of structures and measures them, which takes tens of minutes and needs no accounts. The design campaigns need GPUs and money and are not seed-reproducible, so their tables are tracked and read as-is. Rendering without executing, via `make preview`, uses the cached results in `_freeze/` and needs neither. See [Reproduce this pub](pages/SETUP.qmd) for the full procedure. **Generating new designs** takes three steps: 1. Get a [Modal](https://modal.com) account. Design runs on H100s, as in the [ESMFold2 binder design cookbook](https://github.com/Biohub/esm) this work ports — the cookbook ships a Modal app of its own, and the container image here is built from the cookbook's own `get_base_image`, so the compute path is the upstream one rather than something we invented. 2. Deploy the app: ```bash modal deploy src/analysis/modal_app.py ``` 3. Re-execute with generation switched on: ```bash USE_MODAL=1 make execute ``` This launches only the campaigns whose tables are missing, waits for them, and collects each as soon as its designs finish. `ESMFOLD2_SS_MAX_CONTAINERS` caps how many designs run at once and defaults to 30; set it to match your own GPU quota. The full grid is five targets by three loss arms by thirty seeds, which is 450 designs at 150 optimization steps, and took 78 minutes at that concurrency. **What a rerun will and will not reproduce.** It will not reproduce these designs. The design loop is not seed-reproducible: across two runs of an identically configured arm, no seed reproduced its own result, and per-seed interface pTM moved by 0.14 to 0.20. The optimization is stochastic in ways that a fixed seed does not pin down, including which model of the inversion ensemble is drawn at each step and non-deterministic GPU kernels. What a rerun reproduces is the *conclusions* — the direction and rough size of every effect reported below — which is the claim worth checking. Delete a campaign's directory under `data/campaigns/` to regenerate just that one. ::: ## Question 1: What is ESMFold2's basal α-richness? Placeholder for the read-off. The answer to establish is that it is high: an unsteered campaign produces designs whose residues are predominantly helical, with sheet content at zero for most designs. ### How secondary structure is assigned Labels come from [`pydssp`](https://github.com/ShintaroMinami/PyDSSP), a Kabsch–Sander implementation, collapsed to three states and reported as a fraction of binder residues. Designs are labelled on chain B of the complex the confidence critic predicts; the natural reference is labelled on deposited coordinates. Only residues with backbone N, Cα, C and O present are labelled, so a residue missing from the model is missing from the denominator too. ### The reference set, and why a reference set at all "Helix-rich" needs something to be rich *relative to*. A designed binder's job is to bind, so the comparator should be a protein that is known to bind something — not a monomer in isolation. The reference is therefore the small chain of a natural heterodimer solved in complex with its partner. It is built by `analysis.rcsb.build`, which runs if the table is absent, so the set is reconstructible rather than merely downloadable — and it measures every structure through the same `analysis.secondary_structure` code that measures the designs, rather than a second copy of DSSP. The query is recorded verbatim in `data/reference/natural_binder_query.json` and asks for X-ray entries at 2.5 Å or better with exactly two distinct polymer entities, heteromeric, with a named source organism that is not "synthetic construct", and at least one entity of 60–200 residues — the length range the design loop samples binders from. Results are returned per entity and clustered at 30% sequence identity, keeping one representative per cluster. That yields **2,098 binder entities from 1,813 entries**, at median resolution 2.00 Å. Where both chains of an entry fall in the length range, which is 53% of them, each takes its turn as the binder: 285 entries contribute two rows and 1,528 contribute one. Because designs vary in length and the natural set does too, the comparison below resamples the natural set to match the length distribution of the designs rather than pooling across lengths, since short natural proteins are helix-biased on their own. The natural set is measured, not assumed: **median helix 0.33, median sheet 0.25, and 21% of natural binders have no sheet at all.** That last figure matters for reading the design numbers, because a design with zero sheet is not by itself unusual. :::{.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Caveats on the reference set"} **"Binder" is a label we impose.** In a natural heterodimer neither chain is the binder; both are partners. Calling the 60–200-residue chain the binder is an analogy to the design setting, not a fact about the complex. **Some partners are peptides, not domains.** Target chains run from 8 to 1,020 residues, and 15% are short enough to flag as peptide targets. A 100-residue protein gripping an 8-residue peptide is a different structural problem from a designed minibinder against a folded domain. These are flagged in the table, not removed, so the flag can be used to test sensitivity. **Some interfaces may not be real.** 13% have interfaces small enough to be crystal packing rather than function. Also flagged rather than removed. **"Natural" is approximate.** 1% of binders and 3% of targets look like engineered scaffolds by description. The query excludes chains whose source organism is "synthetic construct", which catches the obvious cases and not the subtle ones. **The PDB is a convenience sample.** Restricting to X-ray at 2.5 Å or better favours proteins that crystallise well, which favours compact, rigid, often β-rich folds, and excludes cryo-EM and NMR entries entirely. The organism distribution is skewed hard toward vertebrates: 31% of binders are human. This is not a sample of natural binding proteins, it is a sample of the ones that got solved. **Clustering at 30% identity does not remove structural redundancy.** Immunoglobulin-like folds recur across clusters that share little sequence. **Composition is measured over resolved residues only**, a median 96% of each construct. Disordered termini and loops are absent from both numerator and denominator, which biases the natural coil fraction downward and makes the natural set look more ordered than the protein is in solution. **The two sides are measured on different kinds of coordinates.** The natural set is experimental; the designs are ESMFold2's own prediction. Predicted structures tend to have idealised secondary structure, which would inflate both helix and sheet in the designs relative to an experimental structure of the same protein. That direction cannot explain the designs' sheet *deficit*, but it does mean the coil comparison should be read loosely. **Clusters can move even though the query cannot.** The query is pinned to entries released on or before 2026-09-02, so the candidate set is fixed. The 30% identity clusters are not ours: the RCSB computes them over the whole present-day PDB and recomputes them as it grows, so which entity represents a cluster can change under a rebuild even when the candidate set does not. Expect a rebuild to reproduce the distribution rather than the exact row set. In the one rebuild done so far it happened to reproduce the row set as well, but that is not something to rely on. ::: Figure 1 goes in the cell below: per-design helix and sheet fraction against binder length, with the length-matched natural set behind it. ::: {#a122fd50 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} natural = reference.composition() designs = composition.load_all(TARGETS, ["vanilla"]) matched = reference.length_matched( natural, designs["binder length (residues)"], "binder_sample_length_residues" ) summary = pd.DataFrame( { "natural binders, length-matched (%)": [ 100 * matched["binder_helix_fraction"].mean(), 100 * matched["binder_sheet_fraction"].mean(), 100 * (matched["binder_sheet_fraction"] == 0).mean(), ], "ESMFold2 vanilla designs (%)": [ 100 * designs["helix (fraction 0-1)"].mean(), 100 * designs["sheet (fraction 0-1)"].mean(), 100 * (designs["sheet (fraction 0-1)"] == 0).mean(), ], }, index=["mean helix", "mean sheet", "designs with zero sheet"], ).round(1) display(summary) fig = figures.composition_vs_length(matched, designs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

The two sections after it do not depend on that answer. ### Summary Placeholder. Two or three sentences: basal α-richness is high, a loss term steers away from it, interface confidence pays for it, and Question 3 decides whether that payment is real. Write this after Question 3 resolves. ### A loss term is a tuning handle, and secondary structure is one thing to tune The steering result matters less for what it does to helices than for what it says about the method. A differentiable term added to the design loss changed the fold class of the output without retraining anything and without touching the model weights. The handle is the distogram the design loop already optimizes against, and it was sitting there unused. That reframes the contribution. This is not a paper about helices. It is a worked example of adding a constraint to ESMFold2's binder design algorithm, with the measurements needed to say honestly what the constraint bought and what it cost. The limits we ran into are part of the example, and they generalize: - The term stops acting once the property it penalizes is already saturated, so **when** a term applies during the run matters as much as how strongly. - Pushing harder on one property costs confidence in another, so any added term needs its tradeoff mapped rather than asserted. - The optimizer will satisfy a loss the cheapest way available, which is not always the way you intended. Anyone adding a term to this design loop should expect all three. ### A binder is the start of a drug program, not the end Nothing in this work produces a therapeutic. A design that binds its target with good predicted confidence has cleared the first of many gates. Downstream, a candidate still has to be developable: expressible and soluble at concentration, stable on the shelf, non-aggregating, humanized or otherwise non-immunogenic, free of manufacturing and post-translational liabilities, and specific enough not to bind everything else in the proteome. Each of those is a property of a sequence or a structure. That is the interesting part, because it is the same kind of object the secondary-structure term acts on. In principle every one of them is expressible as a term on the distogram or on the sequence logits, and added to the same objective in the same place. Sequence liabilities are the nearest example, and one worth tuning rather than ignoring. Steering the fold also changes the sequences that come out, so a term that optimizes structure alone can quietly degrade a property nobody was watching. We did not write a liability term here, and the designs in this work should not be read as developable. Adding one is the obvious next thing to try, and it would test whether the tuning handle generalizes beyond the property we happened to pick. That is the claim we want to leave the reader with: ESMFold2's binder design algorithm exposes a place to put constraints, secondary structure is one constraint that demonstrably works there, and the constraints a drug program actually cares about are the reason to care. ## Next steps Placeholder. What we would do next, and what someone else could pick up. Fill in once the takeaways are settled. ## An open question: objective or weights? Everything here changes behavior without changing the model. The steering happens in the design loop, on top of frozen weights, and that is worth naming as a choice rather than a default, because there is an obvious alternative: retrain or fine-tune so that the model produces the distribution you want natively. The two routes are not equivalent, and our results show some of the difference. Steering from the objective fights the model's prior instead of altering it, which may be why interface confidence pays a price, and why the optimizer sometimes satisfies the term in ways we did not intend. A model whose weights had learned the target distribution would presumably not need to be argued with in the same way. But the comparison is lopsided on cost. Adding a term to the loss is a few lines and a single campaign. Retraining a structure prediction model of this scale means substantial compute, a training corpus assembled for the property you want, and revalidation of everything the base model was already good at, with the risk of degrading it. For a property you might only want occasionally, or want in three mutually exclusive variants, that is a steep price. Post-hoc terms are also composable, inspectable, and trivially reversible, which weight updates are not. So we would pose it as a question rather than answer it. Which behaviors belong in the weights, and which belong in the objective? Is there a principled boundary, drawn perhaps by how fundamental a property is or how often it is wanted, or is the line mostly economic and therefore likely to move as training costs fall? We do not know, and the honest position from this work is that the objective route is cheap enough to be worth exhausting before anyone reaches for the weights.
